deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the draft of the end of §6 and the start of §7 of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, published by Dedekind 1867). The text on this page is essentially the published wording.

(A) End of the discussion of improper integrals at a singular point x=0, continuing the previous page. On that page Riemann showed the following for f without infinitely many maxima and minima near 0. If the integral ∫_x^a f dx converges as x→0, then x f(x) → 0, and likewise x log(1/x) f(x) → 0, x log(1/x) loglog(1/x) f(x) → 0, and so on. Conversely, the integral converges if x^α f(x) → 0 for some α<1, or if the corresponding iterated-log product with exponent α>1 on the last log tends to 0.

This page adds that if f has infinitely many maxima and minima, nothing can be said about the order of growth. Suppose only |f| is prescribed; the order of becoming infinite depends only on |f|. Then one can always choose the sign of f so that ∫_x f dx converges as x→0.

My filling of the implicit argument, assuming |f| is integrable on every [ε,a]: split each block [2^{-k-1}, 2^{-k}] into finitely many pieces of |f|-mass ≤ 1/k each, arranged in an even number with equal mass in pairs. Alternate the sign on consecutive pieces. Then each block contributes 0, and the oscillation of the partial integrals inside the k-th block is ≤ 1/k → 0, so the integral converges.

Example: f(x) = d/dx[x cos(e^{1/x})] = cos(e^{1/x}) + (1/x) e^{1/x} sin(e^{1/x}).
- Its order of infinity, measured in powers of 1/x, is infinite, because of the factor e^{1/x}/x.
- Yet ∫_x^a f dt = a cos(e^{1/a}) − x cos(e^{1/x}) → a cos(e^{1/a}) as x→0, since |x cos(...)| ≤ x.
- So the improper integral exists.
Riemann then remarks that this topic belongs to another field and turns to his main problem.

(B) Start of §7.
- Methodological point: earlier work (Fourier, Dirichlet, ...) aimed to prove the Fourier series for cases arising in nature. Such work could begin with an arbitrary function and later impose restrictions as needed.
- Riemann instead poses the converse question: if a function is representable by a trigonometric series, what follows about its behaviour, i.e. how its value changes as the argument varies continuously?
- He takes the series Ω = ½b_0 + Σ_{n≥1} (a_n sin nx + b_n cos nx), written as two rows. He sets f(x) = value of Ω, defined only where Ω converges.
- A necessary condition for convergence is that the terms tend to 0. So if a_n, b_n do not tend to 0, the series can converge only at x where the trigonometric multipliers of the non-vanishing coefficients are zero.
- This still allows convergence on a set that is dense in every interval.
- Example: if only the coefficients of sin(m! x) stay bounded, or even become infinite, the series can converge at all x commensurable with π. For x = pπ/q, m!·x is a multiple of π once m ≥ q, so sin(m! x) = 0 from then on, and only finitely many such terms are nonzero.
errors: The claim that the sign can always be chosen so the integral converges is stated without proof. It implicitly assumes |f| is integrable on each [ε,a]; under that assumption it is correct by the alternating-sign construction in the reconstruction.

In the sin(m!)x example, 'convergiren können' tacitly requires that the remaining coefficients behave well enough (e.g., tend to zero suitably) for the rest of the series to converge. Riemann hedges with 'können', so this is not an error.

results.what: With infinitely many oscillations, the order of growth of |f| gives no condition for convergence of the improper integral; signs can be chosen to force convergence.
results.modern_name: Conditionally convergent improper integrals / oscillatory cancellation

results.what: Example d/dx[x cos(e^{1/x})]: improperly integrable on (0,a] although it grows faster than any power of 1/x.
results.modern_name: Improper Riemann integral of an unbounded, wildly oscillating function

results.what: Reversal of the problem: from representability by a trigonometric series, deduce properties of the function (start of Riemann's theory of trigonometric series).
results.modern_name: Riemann's theory of general trigonometric series

results.what: Terms must tend to 0. A series with non-decaying coefficients on the indices m! can still converge on the dense set of rational multiples of π.
results.modern_name: Necessary term condition; convergence on dense sets despite non-null coefficients (precursor of Cantor–Lebesgue theorem considerations)

transcription_corrections: The pencil margin note 'dass das Integral' beside line 6 is an editorial or later annotation repeating the phrase in the text, not part of Riemann's sentence.
In 'eine allgemeine Untersuchung' the word 'allgemeine' is an underlined interlinear insertion, consistent with the transcription.
'willkürlichen' is inserted with quotation-like marks in the image; the transcription is otherwise faithful.
The series is written in two rows (sine row above, cosine row below), representing the single series Ω = ½b_0 + Σ(a_n sin nx + b_n cos nx).
